64.title: Not-self, taught
64.hook: to the five: is the body you, is feeling, is any of the five heaps mine (SN 22.59)
64.howItsDone: Some Buddhist meditators reflect on the five aggregates, noting of each 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self', and the Anattalakkhana Sutta is among the suttas chanted in Theravada monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kondañña sees: the first of the five understood that whatever arises, ends. Now a new week: the sangha grows.

Who are you, in one sentence? The answers tend to reach for the same things. My body. My job. My feelings about things. My memories, my opinions, my personality. That's me. A few days after the first sermon, all five companions have understood the basics, and the Buddha sits them down in the Deer Park again. This time he goes after that one sentence. He takes the pieces you point to when you say me, holds each one up to the light, and asks a very simple question about it. It's the second teaching in the old accounts.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU, IN ONE SENTENCE?` → `THE PIECES WE CALL ME.` → `ONE SIMPLE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Not-self. In Pali, anatta. The teaching is called the Discourse on the Characteristic of Not-self, and it works like a careful conversation. First the Buddha names five heaps, the bundles that make up a person as you experience one: the body; feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neither; perception, recognizing things; mental formations, urges and habits; and consciousness, the knowing. Then he asks about the body. If the body were really your self, it wouldn't lead to trouble, and you could just say: let my body be like this, not like that. But you can't. It gets sick. It ages. It doesn't take orders. Is the body permanent or impermanent, he asks. Impermanent, they say. And is something impermanent a source of lasting ease, or of unease? Unease. Then is it right to look at it and say, this is mine, this I am, this is my self? No, they say. He asks the same of feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Same answers every time. The texts say that as the five heard this, their minds were freed. Two things are worth knowing. First, it's a practice more than a philosophy: you look at a feeling and ask, is this me, is this mine? The looking is the point. Second, Buddhist schools read it in different ways. But notice what the sutta never says: that you don't exist. Your body, your moods, your thoughts are all really happening. None of them is a fixed owner sitting in the middle, holding the others. There's no one piece you could point to and say, that, forever, is me.
screen: `FIVE HEAPS MAKE A PERSON.` · `IS IT PERMANENT? IS IT MINE?` · `THE SAME QUESTION, FIVE TIMES.` · `NOT 'YOU DON'T EXIST.'` · then, large: `NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Notice whatever feeling is here right now, tiredness, worry, a little boredom, contentment, and find it in the body if you can. Then ask it gently, are you me, did I choose you, will you stay, and watch it while you ask. There's no answer to get right; just notice what happens to a feeling when you stop assuming it's you.
Not-self. Anatta: no body, feeling, perception, habit or knowing that you can hold up and say, this, forever, is mine.
Your line: not mine. The feeling is real; it just isn't the owner. That's day sixty-four.

65.title: Yasa's night
65.hook: a rich young man wakes after a party, sickened, and walks out into the night (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1)
65.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Yasa's story as one of the first conversions after the Deer Park, and remember his father as the first lay follower to take refuge in the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, as lay Buddhists still do today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not-self: five heaps, and none of them a fixed owner. Not mine.

Three in the morning. The party's over, but nobody went home. People asleep on the cushions, on the floor, one still clutching a lute. The music stopped a while ago. One young man is awake, looking at it all, and something turns in his stomach that isn't the food. His name is Yasa, son of a very rich family in Benares, with a house for every season and musicians who played for him through the night. Tonight he woke before everyone else.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `THE ONLY ONE AWAKE.` → `A RICH YOUNG MAN NAMED YASA.`

segments.voice: The old monastic rulebook, the Vinaya, tells it vividly. The lamps are still burning, and Yasa sees the musicians and attendants asleep around him, sprawled in every direction, mouths open, instruments dropped. The text says it looked to him like a cemetery. He cries out: how distressing this is, how oppressive. He puts on his golden slippers and walks out of the house, out of the city gate, into the dark, toward the Deer Park. And the Buddha, the story says, is walking up and down in the open air before dawn. He hears Yasa's cry and answers: this is not distressing, this is not oppressive. Come, Yasa, sit down. I'll teach you. So a young man in party clothes and golden slippers sits on the ground with a wandering teacher, listens, and something in him settles. Some readers notice how much it sounds like another story. A young man of a rich family, pleasure all around him, a night when he looks at sleeping bodies and sees the truth under the glitter, a walk out into the dark. That's the Buddha's own going forth. Yasa lives it in one night, and this time someone is waiting on the road. And his name, Yasa, means fame, or glory. The man named Fame found the party empty. It doesn't stop with him. His father comes searching, following the tracks of those golden slippers, and becomes the first lay follower to take the three refuges. His mother and his former wife become the first women lay followers. And Yasa's friends come looking for him too. Tomorrow, where that leads.
screen: `IT LOOKED LIKE A CEMETERY.` · `COME, YASA, SIT DOWN.` · `THE BUDDHA'S STORY IN ONE NIGHT.` · `HIS FAMILY FOLLOWS THE SLIPPERS.` · then, large: `WALK OUT OF THE PARTY.`

segments.voice: Think of something you keep doing that doesn't give you what it used to: an app you open without meaning to, a habit gone flat, a place you go because you always have. Picture it the way Yasa saw that room, with the lamps still on. You don't have to hate it; just see it clearly, and imagine standing up and walking out the door.
Yasa's night. A rich young man wakes after a party, sees it clearly, walks out into the dark, and finds the Buddha on the road.
Your line: walk out of the party. Golden slippers, a dark road, and a teacher at the end of it. Until tomorrow.

66.title: The Kalamas ask
66.hook: a town tired of teachers asks the Buddha whom to believe; he ends with four comforts that hold whether or not there is a next life (AN 3.65)
66.howItsDone: Teachers often quote the Kalama Sutta to newcomers who are unsure about rebirth; many Buddhist communities welcome people to practice while the question is still open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasa's night: a rich young man walked out of a party at three in the morning, and found someone waiting on the road.
screen: `YASA'S NIGHT — WALK OUT OF THE PARTY.`

segments.voice: Yasa's friends come, then fifty more, and soon the Buddha sends them all walking, for the good of the many. The roads of India are full of walking teachers. In a town called Kesaputta, the people, the Kalamas, have had enough. Teacher after teacher comes through, praises his own teaching, and runs down everyone else's. Then the next one does the same. And when the Buddha arrives, they put it to him plainly: we don't know who to believe. Even about whether there's another life at all.
screen: `SENT WALKING, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.` → `TEACHER AFTER TEACHER.` → `WHO DO WE BELIEVE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha's first answer surprises them. Your doubt is reasonable, he says. You're right to be unsure. He goes on to give them a way to test any teaching, and we'll come back to that later on the path. Today is about the way the talk ends, the part people often skip. He describes someone whose mind is free of hatred and ill will, clear and clean. That person, he says, has four comforts, right here in this life. If there is another world, and good and bad deeds bear fruit, then I'll arise somewhere good. If there isn't, then here and now I live free of hostility, at ease. If harm comes to those who do harm, I intend harm to no one, so how could it touch me? And if it doesn't, I'm clean either way. The Pali word is assasa: comfort, the kind that lets you breathe out. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell the Kalamas to settle the question of rebirth before they begin. Rebirth runs all through his teaching, and many Buddhists hold it close. But this talk starts with what anyone can see. Teachers read it in more than one way. Some say the Buddha is meeting doubters where they are, before he teaches more. Others take it as a welcome to begin with the question still open. Either way, the Kalamas walk away with something they can use tomorrow morning. And if you're not sure about rebirth yet, you're in company the Buddha himself sat down with.
screen: `YOUR DOUBT IS REASONABLE.` · `IF THERE IS ANOTHER LIFE, IT GOES WELL.` · `IF THERE ISN'T, THIS ONE ALREADY DOES.` · `BEGIN WITH THE QUESTION OPEN.` · then, large: `GOOD EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one big question you can't settle, about what comes after or anything else, and don't try to answer it; picture setting it down beside you, still there, still open. Then notice what is true without the answer: the breath coming in, the breath going out, and the chance, today, to act without ill will.
Assasa. Comfort, relief, a breath let out: the four comforts the Buddha gave the Kalamas, which hold whether or not there is another life.
Your line: good either way. A life without ill will is good whether or not there's another one. Day sixty-six, done.

67.title: The fire sermon
67.hook: to a thousand fire-worshipers: all is burning, with greed, hate and delusion (SN 35.28)
67.howItsDone: The Fire Sermon (Adittapariyaya Sutta) is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and Buddhist teachers use its three fires, greed, hatred and delusion, to explain what nibbana puts out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, assasa: the Kalamas asked whom to believe, and the Buddha gave them four comforts that hold either way.

Coaches talk in plays. Musicians talk in songs. The way into a room is often through what it already knows. The Buddha has walked back to Uruvela, near the tree of his awakening, and meets three brothers named Kassapa: famous teachers with matted hair, who with their followers number about a thousand. Their whole religious life is tending sacred fires, keeping the flames going, making offerings into them. The old texts tell of wonders and long nights before the brothers are won over; then they throw their hair and their fire tools into the river. Afterward he leads all thousand up a hill called Gaya Head, looking out over the land. And to people who have spent their lives watching fire, he talks about fire.
screen: `TALK TO YOUR OWN CROWD.` → `A THOUSAND WHO TENDED FIRES.` → `UP THE HILL AT GAYA HEAD.`

segments.voice: It begins, in the texts, with one stark sentence: everything, monks, is burning. And what is burning? The eye, what the eye sees, the seeing itself. The ear, and sounds. The nose, and smells. The tongue, the body, the mind, and everything they touch. Burning with what? With the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. With birth, aging and death, with sorrow and grief and despair. Hear it as a fire-keeper would. You've fed flames every day of your life, and now someone points at your own eyes and says: there's the fire. You don't have to climb a hill to find it. It's in the wanting, the anger, the confusion. Then the turn. Someone who sees this, he says, grows tired of feeding it. They become disenchanted, and cool. The wanting fades, and with its fading, they are free. The texts say that as they listened, the thousand were freed too. Some teachers connect that cooling to nibbana, nirvana, a word Pali also uses for a fire going out, the way a lamp goes out when its oil is used up. And it traveled a long way. In 1922, the poet T. S. Eliot named a whole section of The Waste Land The Fire Sermon, and ended it with the word burning, over and over. A talk on a hill in India turned up in a famous poem in English.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS BURNING.` · `GREED, HATRED, DELUSION.` · `SEE IT, AND IT COOLS.` · `A SERMON IN A MODERN POEM.` · then, large: `ALL IS BURNING.`

segments.voice: Scan yourself slowly, like checking a house for heat: wanting that pulls toward a screen, a snack, a person; irritation, a hot spot about something someone said; fog, a place you'd rather not look. Don't fight any of it; just find the warm places and name them, wanting, anger, fog. Then breathe out slowly, as if you were cooling soup.
Aditta. Burning: taught to a thousand fire-keepers on Gaya Head, the senses burn with greed, hatred and delusion, and seeing it lets them cool.
Your line: all is burning. Seeing the fire is where the cooling starts. Rest well.

68.title: Sariputta and Moggallana
68.hook: Assaji's short verse: things arise from a cause, and the Buddha tells their cause; Sariputta understands at once
68.howItsDone: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples, often shown standing on either side of him in temples, and Assaji's verse, 'ye dhamma hetuppabhava', is still chanted and has been inscribed on stupas, seals and images across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, aditta, burning, on Gaya Head: greed, hatred and delusion, and the cooling that comes from seeing them.

Two best friends make a pact: whoever finds the answer first tells the other. Upatissa and Kolita grew up together, sons of important families near the city of Rajagaha. As young men they went to a festival, looked at the crowds laughing and the actors on stage, and both thought the same thing: in a hundred years, none of these people will be alive. So they left home together to search for what doesn't die. They studied with a famous teacher, learned everything he had, and it wasn't enough. Then one morning in Rajagaha, Upatissa sees a monk walking for alms.
screen: `WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST, TELLS.` → `A HUNDRED YEARS FROM NOW.` → `A MONK IN THE STREET.`

segments.voice: The monk is Assaji, one of the five from the Deer Park. What catches Upatissa's eye is the way he walks: calm, collected, eyes down, every movement settled. Upatissa follows him, waits politely until he's finished his meal, and asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji is honest. I'm new, he says. I can't explain the teaching at length, but I can tell you the gist. And he says a single verse, four short lines. In paraphrase: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and also how they cease. That's the teaching of the great one. Hearing it, the texts say, Upatissa's dhamma eye opened, the same clear seeing Kondañña had: whatever arises, ceases. He runs to Kolita, who sees his face and knows at once. Did you find it? Upatissa repeats the verse, and Kolita understands too. The pact is kept. They go to the Buddha together, with many of their old teacher's students. Upatissa becomes known as Sariputta, son of Sari, his mother's name. Kolita becomes Moggallana. They become the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta known for wisdom, Moggallana for deep meditation powers. That little verse, in Pali ye dhamma hetuppabhava, became one of the most copied lines in the Buddhist world. It's been found carved on stones, stamped on clay seals, and set inside statues and stupas across Asia, as a summary of the whole teaching. The Dhammapada says one word of sense, which brings peace to the hearer, is better than a thousand empty ones.
screen: `THE WAY ASSAJI WALKED.` · `I CAN ONLY GIVE THE GIST.` · `THE PACT IS KEPT.` · `ONE VERSE, CARVED ACROSS ASIA.` · then, large: `ONE VERSE WAS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Think back over what's helped you, here or anywhere: a saying, a verse, a sentence someone said at the right moment, and pick just one. Say it silently a few times, and feel why it helped. Then picture one person who might need it, and hold just the line for them, no lecture, the way Assaji gave it.
Sariputta. One of two friends who kept their pact, and became the Buddha's chief disciples, after hearing one short verse from the monk Assaji.
Your line: one verse was enough. Four short lines, and two friends kept their pact. Sixty-eight days now.

69.title: Coming home
69.hook: he returns to Kapilavatthu; young Rahula asks for his inheritance and is given the teaching
69.howItsDone: In some Theravada countries boys spend a time as novices, with Rahula as their model, and the monastic code asks for parents' permission before a child is ordained, a rule traced to King Suddhodana's request.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputta and Moggallana: two friends, one pact, and Assaji's four-line verse. One verse was enough.

Going home after years away is its own kind of nervous. The streets look smaller. Everyone knows the old you. Remember the night Siddhartha left Kapilavatthu: the palace, his wife Yasodhara asleep, their newborn son Rahula beside her. He didn't wake them. Now, years later, the story goes, word reaches his father, King Suddhodana, that his son has become a famous teacher. The king sends messengers begging him to visit, and he comes. But not the way a prince comes home. He walks into his hometown with a crowd of monks, and in the morning does what monks do: house to house with a bowl, asking for food.
screen: `THE STREETS LOOK SMALLER.` → `THE KING SENDS FOR HIM.` → `A PRINCE WITH A BOWL.`

segments.voice: Later tradition fills in the scene. The king is mortified. My son, begging, in my own city? Our family has never done this. The Buddha answers that his family now is the line of Buddhas before him, and this is their custom. Then comes the moment the old monastic texts do record. Rahula is a small boy now. His mother, Yasodhara, sends him to his father with a message: go and ask him for your inheritance. So the boy stands close to the teacher everyone's talking about, and the texts say he told him, pleasant is your shadow, monk. When the Buddha gets up and walks away, Rahula follows: give me my inheritance, monk. Give me my inheritance. The Buddha doesn't hand over land, or gold, or a crown. He turns to Sariputta, the wise friend from yesterday, and asks him to ordain the boy. Rahula becomes a novice, a young monk in training. The reasoning, as the commentaries tell it: the wealth he's asking for brings trouble and ends; I'll give him an inheritance that doesn't. The texts are honest that this hurt. King Suddhodana, who had already lost two sons to the homeless life, now loses his grandson too. He goes to the Buddha and says: when you left home, it was pain. When Nanda left, the same. And now Rahula. Please, don't let children be ordained without their parents' permission. The Buddha agrees, and makes it a rule: no child is to be ordained without a parent's consent. One family's grief, written into the monastic code for every family after.
screen: `A PRINCE WITH A BOWL.` · `GIVE ME MY INHERITANCE.` · `THE BOY IS GIVEN THE TEACHING.` · `A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.` · then, large: `THE REAL INHERITANCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you inherited that wasn't money: a way of laughing, how someone fixed things, a saying, a recipe, a habit of patience. Trace it back: who gave it to you, and who gave it to them? Stay with that line of hands, as far back as it goes.
Coming home. The Buddha returns to Kapilavatthu with a bowl, and his son Rahula, asking for an inheritance, is given the teaching.
Your line: the real inheritance. Not land or gold, but the teaching. Day sixty-nine, and nearly seventy.

70.title: The women ask
70.hook: Mahapajapati and many women shave their heads and walk to ask for ordination; Ananda speaks for them
70.tomorrow: the man with the finger garland
70.howItsDone: Buddhist nuns live in monastic communities in many countries; fully ordained bhikkhunis are found especially in Chinese, Korean, Taiwanese and Vietnamese traditions, and in growing but debated numbers in Theravada countries, while many Buddhist women also live as novices or precept-holding renunciants.

segments.voice: Yesterday, coming home: Rahula asked for his inheritance and was given the teaching. The real inheritance.

Some doors have to be knocked on more than once. Mahapajapati Gotami was the Buddha's aunt. When his mother died, she raised him as her own. Years later, in Kapilavatthu, she asked him: let women go forth too, into the homeless life, as nuns. He said no. She asked again. No. A third time. No. She went away weeping. But she didn't stop. When he left for the city of Vesali, she cut off her hair, put on the ochre robes, and set out walking after him. And she didn't go alone.

segments.voice: Many women of the Sakya clan walk with her, heads shaved, robed. At Vesali, the old text describes her standing outside the gate of the hall: feet swollen, body covered in dust, in tears. Ananda, the Buddha's cousin and attendant, finds her there and asks what's wrong. She tells him, and Ananda goes in to ask for them. The answer is no, three times. Then Ananda tries a different question. Lord, are women able, if they go forth, to reach the fruits of the path, all the way to full awakening? Yes, Ananda, they are. Ananda presses on: then think of Mahapajapati, who nursed you, fed you her own milk when your mother died. And the Buddha agrees. Women may be ordained. Today's word is what they became: bhikkhuni, a fully ordained Buddhist nun, the feminine of bhikkhu, monk. The texts also say women were given eight extra rules, placing nuns under the monks in certain ways. Buddhists and scholars today discuss those rules and their history. What happened to the order afterward differs by place. Full ordination for nuns continued unbroken in Chinese, Korean, Taiwanese and Vietnamese communities. In Theravada countries the line lapsed long ago; in recent decades some have revived it, and others in those traditions do not accept the revival. In Tibetan communities, full ordination for women has long been debated. And the early nuns left something of their own: the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, where women tell of their awakening in their own voices. This week: not-self, Yasa's night, the Kalamas, aditta, two friends and one verse, coming home, and today, the women who walked.
